templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Ophiolites, slabs of ocean crust and upper mantle pushed onto continents by colliding plates, let geologists examine rocks that formed beneath the seafloor. ______ most ophiolites were fractured and tilted as they rose, scrambling the original order of their layers. Still, in Oman’s Semail ophiolite, the complete sequence, from mantle peridotite to seafloor basalt, remains largely intact.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a claim in favor of ophiolites: they “let geologists examine rocks that formed beneath the seafloor.” The blank sentence then concedes a weakness that cuts against that claim: most ophiolites “were fractured and tilted as they rose, scrambling the original order of their layers.” The next sentence returns to the main point with “Still,” pointing to the Semail ophiolite, where “the complete sequence” “remains largely intact.” “Granted” fits, since it introduces a point the writer admits before going back to the claim.

A.why_wrong: The fracturing and tilting of most ophiolites do not spell out how ophiolites let geologists examine deep rocks; they are a drawback the writer concedes, which is why the next sentence opens with “Still.”

B.why_wrong: The damaged layers are not a further point in favor of ophiolites; they limit the first sentence’s claim, and “Still” then sets that limit aside.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not describe a case like the one in the first sentence; it describes a problem with most ophiolites, which the writer concedes before turning to the exception in Oman.

items.notes: Grant then turn on the 3.19 / f5959727 shape (supported claim, concession in the blank sentence, Still resumes with an exception that rescues the claim), keyed Granted (K1 live keys: of course 14, granted 8, admittedly 4). Traps: Moreover and Specifically for a reader who takes the blank sentence as more information about ophiolites rather than a drawback. items.passage: Astronomers attribute the Geminid meteor shower not to an icy comet, the customary source of such showers, but to 3200 Phaethon, a rocky asteroid. The meteoroids’ trajectories nearly coincide with Phaethon’s orbit, and the asteroid has been observed expelling dust during its closest approaches to the Sun. ______ the material Phaethon currently releases is far too sparse to account for the stream’s considerable mass.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences build a case that Phaethon is the source of the Geminids: the meteoroids’ trajectories “nearly coincide with Phaethon’s orbit,” and the asteroid “has been observed expelling dust.” The blank sentence then adds a fact that limits that case without overturning it: the material Phaethon releases now “is far too sparse to account for the stream’s considerable mass.” “That said” fits, since it introduces a qualification of a point the writer has just supported.

A.why_wrong: The shortage of dust is not a result of the matching orbits or of Phaethon’s shedding; it is a problem for the claim those facts support.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not single out one particular case of the shedding just described; it says the shedding is too slight to explain the stream, which weakens rather than illustrates the point before it.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not one more piece of evidence linking Phaethon to the Geminids; it is a fact that complicates that link.

items.passage: For decades, engineer Charles Bliss promoted his pictographic symbols as a universal script that speakers of any language could read. Yet despite a lengthy 1949 guide and repeated appeals to officials, the system attracted few users. ______ Blissymbols found an enduring purpose Bliss had never envisioned: in the early 1970s, Toronto educators adapted them for children with cerebral palsy who could not speak.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe a long, mostly unsuccessful effort: Bliss promoted his symbols for decades, yet “the system attracted few users.” The blank sentence gives the outcome in which that story ends: “Blissymbols found an enduring purpose Bliss had never envisioned.” “Ultimately” fits, since it introduces what in the end became of the symbols after years of failed promotion.

A.why_wrong: The system’s failure to attract users is not the reason educators adapted it for children who could not speak; the passage gives no causal link between the two.

C.why_wrong: The educators did not adapt the symbols in order to serve the goal of a script for speakers of any language; the passage says the use they found was one “Bliss had never envisioned.”

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not one more fact of the same kind as Bliss’s promotion of the script; it gives the way that story finally turned out, a use quite unlike the one he intended.

items.passage: In 2008, researchers reported a bacterium that subsists on chemicals generated when radiation from the surrounding rock splits water molecules. The microbe lives entirely alone in fluid from a fracture nearly 3 kilometers deep in South Africa’s Mponeng gold mine. ______ it was named Desulforudis audaxviator, after a line in Jules Verne’s Journey to the Center of the Earth urging a “bold traveler” to descend.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence before the blank stresses how deep the bacterium lives: “nearly 3 kilometers deep” in a gold mine. The blank sentence then reports a name that suits that fact, since it comes from a novel about a journey to the center of the Earth and a line that urges a “bold traveler” to descend. “Fittingly” fits, since it signals that the name is an apt match for what the first sentence describes.

B.why_wrong: The name is not simply one more fact about how the bacterium lives; the point of the blank sentence is that the name suits the microbe’s deep home.

C.why_wrong: Nothing earlier in the passage would make a name about descending surprising; the name matches the microbe’s depth instead of holding despite it.

D.why_wrong: The naming is not an instance of the claim that the microbe “subsists on chemicals generated when radiation from the surrounding rock splits water molecules”; it is a separate fact that echoes the microbe’s depth.

items.notes: Aptness on the 3.13 / 1e31470f and 2.5 shape (a notable fact, then a fitting echo), keyed Fittingly (P1 hard live keys: to that end 10, fittingly 6). P1 has no band-7 official items, so band_target is 6 as planned. No cause decoy (aptness and cause exclude each other, since the deep home is in a sense why the name was chosen) and no In fact or Indeed. Traps: Moreover for a reader who takes the name as one more detail, For instance for a reader who reads the name as part of the description. Verne’s line is “Descende, audax viator, et terrestre centrum attinges”; the passage quotes only “bold traveler”. The 2008 genome study (Chivian et al., Science) is described without naming its authors. items.passage: The Kokinshū (c. 905), the first imperially commissioned anthology of Japanese poetry, opens with a preface by Ki no Tsurayuki. In it, Tsurayuki likens poetry to countless leaves of words sprouting from a single seed, the human heart. ______ the preface appraises six poets of the preceding generation individually, commending and criticizing each, making it an early landmark of Japanese literary criticism.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence describes one feature of Tsurayuki’s preface: in it, he “likens poetry to countless leaves of words sprouting from a single seed, the human heart.” The blank sentence describes a second, separate feature of the same preface: it “appraises six poets of the preceding generation individually.” “What’s more” fits, since it adds a further point about the preface rather than explaining or limiting the first.

A.why_wrong: Appraising six earlier poets does not spell out the image of poetry growing from the heart like leaves from a seed; it is a different thing the preface does.

B.why_wrong: Commending and criticizing earlier poets does not qualify or cut against the preface’s view of where poetry comes from; the two points sit side by side.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the seed-and-leaves image; it reports new content, the preface’s judgments of six poets.

items.passage: In Japan, envelopes containing monetary gifts are often tied with mizuhiki, decorative cords of tightly twisted paper. For weddings, the cords are fastened in a knot that cannot be undone, signifying that the occasion should happen only once. A bow-shaped knot, ______ can be untied and retied effortlessly, so it adorns gifts celebrating births and other occasions people hope will recur.

items.explanation: The second sentence describes the knot used for weddings, one “that cannot be undone,” chosen because a wedding “should happen only once.” The blank sentence describes a second knot with the opposite qualities: a bow-shaped knot “can be untied and retied effortlessly” and adorns gifts for occasions “people hope will recur.” “In contrast” fits, since it marks the bow-shaped knot as different from the wedding knot.

A.why_wrong: The bow-shaped knot is not an example of the knot that cannot be undone; it is the opposite kind of knot.

C.why_wrong: The bow-shaped knot is not like the wedding knot: one cannot be undone, and the other can be untied and retied.

D.why_wrong: Nothing about the wedding knot causes a bow-shaped knot to be easy to untie; the sentence sets up a difference, not a result.

items.notes: Two subjects with opposite values, the contrast connective as an interrupter after the subject (2.6, 1.34), keyed in contrast (C1 medium live keys: by contrast 29, in contrast 13). Musubikiri for weddings and the bow knot (cho musubi) for repeatable celebrations is standard gift etiquette. items.passage: In Purity and Danger (1966), anthropologist Mary Douglas observed that shoes are not considered dirty in themselves but become so when placed on a dining table.
